comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 programme catalogue confirms 45 EC of first-year required courses, an 85 EC major, 10 EC electives, 30 EC flexible space and 10 EC Global Citizenship. In the first year students also take three 5 EC choices, one of which counts toward another degree requirement. The major catalogue gives the classes of 2026 and 2027 a 45 EC major choice block and 10 EC capstone. The class of 2028 has 40 EC and a 15 EC capstone. The current catalogue does not expressly state the Culture, History and Society major rule for September 2026 entrants, expected to graduate in 2029. The stored upper-year components preserve a reference example under the older rule for further research. Only the seven confirmed compulsory first-year components are selected for display.

alternativeSelection.assessment: The closest option integrates historical inquiry, interpretation of cultural forms and analysis of social relations. The Earth systems option develops the formal sustainability direction. A governance option connects the formal development, justice and world politics directions through a shared focus on how institutions respond to global problems. Three academically distinct options meet the programme requirements. The health major lacks a corresponding generator-eligible interest in this target.

comparisonAlignment.rationale: UCR teaches calculus and linear algebra as quantitative foundations; Leiden applies mathematics specifically to social networks, which the UCR course does not cover.
UCR develops academic writing in Personal & Professional Development and rhetoric. Leiden has a dedicated introductory academic writing course.
Leiden begins with a dedicated interdisciplinary course about global challenges. UCR addresses those questions through subject courses across the three options.
UCR offers beginner Dutch and practical communication. Leiden combines Dutch language with a history and culture component.
Research Methods & Statistics introduces descriptive and inferential statistics alongside research design. Leiden teaches introductory statistics as a separate first-year course.
Leiden combines academic study of global challenges with local engagement in a dedicated course. UCR develops community engagement skills and uses local projects in selected courses.
Leiden allows a 10 EC Spanish beginner course in its Global Citizenship requirement. This UCR selection includes beginner Dutch.
Both introduce historical transformations that shaped modern societies. UCR starts in 1815 and traces industry, sovereignty and social change.
Both apply philosophical reasoning to present-day ethical questions. UCR concentrates on moral theories and practical ethical judgment.
Both use social theory to interpret everyday social life. UCR also introduces sociological research and studies class, race and gender.
Leiden’s course studies digital forms of social life; the UCR social-theory course addresses civil society and decolonial critiques, not that digital focus.
Leiden’s infrastructure, art and culture course has a distinct organising subject; UCR’s broad archaeology of ancient crafts is not presented as its direct match.
Both examine how power and racialisation shape representation. UCR concentrates on storytelling in media and its historical contexts.
UCR examines cultural expression through literary and media analysis and studies social differences in sociology. Leiden introduces cultural study as a distinct field.
UCR studies adaptation across text and film. Leiden specifically studies how cultural meanings are translated across contexts.
UCR examines imperial power and colonial legacies. Leiden asks how scientific practices and knowledge developed in imperial settings.
UCR investigates identity, inequality and social differences in sociology. Leiden approaches difference through anthropology.
UCR studies empires and global politics across several courses. Leiden follows a dedicated modern Asian history sequence in this course.
UCR examines media, racial representation and how historical experiences are remembered. Leiden studies the politics of cultural memory as its organising subject.
UCR studies waste through material recovery and remediation. Leiden approaches waste through its cultural and social meanings.
Both develop source-based historical inquiry. Leiden focuses on testimony, while UCR develops a substantial historical research paper.
Both use qualitative research design and interpretation. UCR includes a small team inquiry and reflection on ethics and positionality.
Leiden requires a research design course in the major. UCR builds research design through qualitative methods and research assignments.
Leiden requires a major capstone. UCR’s optional independent research sits outside the displayed 180 EC schedule.
